title: Rotate List
approach_name: Make a cycle then break at new tail
notes:
Task and constraints: Rotate a singly linked list right by k positions. The list may be empty, and k can exceed the number of nodes.
Idea: Count the nodes, connect the tail to the head to form a cycle, reduce k modulo the length, then break the cycle after n-k steps from the old head.
Technique and why it applies: A right rotation moves the final k nodes to the front; a cycle makes that cut a simple pointer operation.
Invariant: Before breaking the cycle, every original node appears exactly once on the circular list.
Edge cases: Empty and one-node lists are unchanged. If k is a multiple of the length, the result is the original order.
Complexity: Time is O(n) to count and locate the cut. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The list is counted and the new tail is located with a constant number of pointers.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def rotateRight(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or not head.next or k == 0: return head
        n=1;tail=head
        while tail.next:tail=tail.next;n+=1
        k%=n
        if k==0:return head
        tail.next=head
        steps=n-k;new_tail=head
        for _ in range(steps-1):new_tail=new_tail.next
        new_head=new_tail.next;new_tail.next=None
        return new_head

title: Unique Paths
notes:
Task and constraints: Count paths from the top-left to bottom-right of an m by n grid when each move is right or down. The answer can grow quickly but fits the problem's return type.
Idea: Use a one-dimensional DP array where dp[c] counts paths to the current row's column. Each cell combines paths from above (old dp[c]) and left (updated dp[c-1]).
Technique and why it applies: Every path to a cell must enter from exactly one of those two predecessors.
Invariant: Before updating column c, dp[c] is the count from above and dp[c-1] is the count from the left in the current row.
Edge cases: A one-row or one-column grid has exactly one path. Initialize every column to one for the first row.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each grid cell updates one DP entry, and only one row is retained.

title: Unique Paths II
notes:
Task and constraints: Count right/down paths through a grid where 1 marks an obstacle and 0 marks an open cell. A path cannot enter an obstacle.
Idea: Maintain dp[c], the number of paths reaching the current cell. An obstacle resets that count to zero; otherwise add the paths from the left to the count from above.
Technique and why it applies: Each open cell receives paths only from its top and left neighbors, while an obstacle blocks every path through that position.
Invariant: After processing a cell, dp[c] equals the number of valid paths from the origin to that cell.
Edge cases: If the start is blocked, all path counts remain zero. A blocked destination also yields zero.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: A single DP row is updated in place while scanning the grid.

title: Minimum Path Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum sum path through a non-negative grid from top-left to bottom-right, moving only right or down.
Idea: Use dp[c] for the minimum cost to reach the current row's cell. The new value is the cell cost plus the minimum of the path from above and the path from the left.
Technique and why it applies: Every valid path enters a cell from its top or left neighbor, so taking the cheaper predecessor is optimal.
Invariant: dp[c] stores the minimum path cost to the current cell after its value is updated.
Edge cases: The first row accumulates from the left; the first column accumulates from above. A one-cell grid returns its own value.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each cell updates a single DP value in a one-row array.

title: Valid Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a string is a valid decimal number, allowing an optional sign, decimal point, and exponent with its own optional sign. The entire trimmed string must follow the grammar.
Idea: Trim outer spaces and validate against a grammar that permits digits with an optional decimal point and an optional exponent whose value contains at least one digit.
Technique and why it applies: The grammar can be expressed precisely with a regular expression, avoiding ambiguous ad hoc checks for each character.
Invariant: The method returns true only if the complete trimmed string matches the numeric grammar; partial matches are rejected.
Edge cases: Accept forms such as .9, 4., +3.14, and -90E3. Reject '.', '+.', '1e', and 'e3'.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for a fixed regex grammar. Extra space is O(n) for the trimmed representation and regex processing.
complexity_reason: The expression scans the trimmed string once under a fixed grammar.

title: Plus One
approach_name: Propagate carry from the last digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Add one to a non-negative integer represented by its decimal digits, with the most significant digit first and no leading zeroes.
Idea: Walk from the last digit toward the front. If a digit is below nine, increment it and return; otherwise set it to zero and continue carrying.
Technique and why it applies: Decimal addition changes only the trailing run of nines and possibly creates one new leading digit.
Invariant: After processing a suffix of nines, that suffix has become zeroes and the carry is still one.
Edge cases: If every digit is nine, allocate a result one element longer with a leading one.
Complexity: Time is O(n) in the worst case. Extra space is O(1) when no leading digit is needed, otherwise O(n) for the new array.
space_complexity: O(1) usual case; O(n) when a new leading digit is needed
complexity_reason: Only a suffix is touched unless every digit is nine.

title: Add Binary
notes:
Task and constraints: Add two binary strings and return their binary sum as a string. Input lengths can be up to 10,000, so converting to machine integers is unsafe.
Idea: Walk both strings from right to left, add available bits and carry, append total modulo two, and update carry by integer division by two.
Technique and why it applies: This is ordinary base-two column addition and handles arbitrarily long strings without parsing the whole number.
Invariant: The reversed output contains the correct low-order sum bits processed so far, and carry is the amount passed to the next position.
Edge cases: The strings may have different lengths. Append a final carry if present, then reverse the output.
Complexity: Time is O(max(m,n)). Extra space is O(max(m,n)) for the output buffer.
complexity_reason: Each input bit is consumed once and each output bit is appended once.

title: Text Justification
approach_name: Greedily pack words and distribute spaces
notes:
Task and constraints: Format words into lines of exactly maxWidth characters with full justification, except the final line and single-word lines, which are left-justified.
Idea: Greedily select the largest word range that fits. Distribute spaces evenly between words, giving extra spaces to leftmost gaps; for the last or single-word line, join with one space and pad right.
Technique and why it applies: The greedy packing rule determines line membership, and integer division/remainder determines balanced spacing.
Invariant: Every completed line contains the earliest unplaced words that fit and has exactly maxWidth characters.
Edge cases: A single-word line receives trailing spaces. The last line uses single spaces between words and trailing padding.
Complexity: Time is O(total input characters plus output size). Space is O(output size) for the returned lines.
complexity_reason: Each word is packed once and each output character is emitted once.

title: Sqrt(x)
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the floor of the square root of a non-negative integer x without using built-in square-root or exponent functions.
Idea: Binary-search an integer candidate between zero and x, keeping the largest candidate whose square does not exceed x.
Technique and why it applies: The predicate candidate^2 <= x is monotonic, so binary search finds its final true value.
Invariant: Every value at or below left is feasible and every value at or above right is infeasible under the half-open search convention.
Edge cases: x=0 and x=1 return themselves. Use division comparison mid <= x // mid to avoid multiplication overflow, with mid zero handled by the bounds.
Complexity: Time is O(log x). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Binary search halves the candidate range each iteration.

title: Climbing Stairs
notes:
Task and constraints: Count ways to reach step n when each move climbs one or two steps. n is at most 45.
Idea: The ways to reach step i are the sum of ways to reach i-1 and i-2. Keep only those two previous counts while iterating upward.
Technique and why it applies: The final move is either one step from i-1 or two steps from i-2, and these choices are disjoint.
Invariant: The two variables hold the number of ways to reach the previous two stair counts.
Edge cases: n=1 returns one and n=2 returns two. Initialize the recurrence to match these base cases.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Only two previous recurrence values are stored.

title: Simplify Path
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert an absolute Unix-style path into its canonical form. Repeated slashes collapse, a dot means the current directory, and two dots move to the parent when possible.
Idea: Split on slashes and use a stack of directory names. Ignore empty components and '.', pop for '..' when possible, and push ordinary names.
Technique and why it applies: Path components are processed in order; moving to a parent reverses the most recent directory entry, which is naturally stack behavior.
Invariant: The stack represents the canonical directory path after processing all components seen so far.
Edge cases: Attempts to move above root are ignored. A path containing only slashes or dot components simplifies to '/'.
Complexity: Time is O(n) over the path characters. Extra space is O(n) for components and the stack.
complexity_reason: Each path component is pushed or popped at most once.

title: Edit Distance
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum insertions, deletions, and replacements needed to transform word1 into word2.
Idea: Let dp[i][j] be the minimum edit distance between the first i characters of word1 and the first j characters of word2. Equal final characters use the diagonal state; otherwise take one plus the minimum of delete, insert, and replace states.
Technique and why it applies: The last operation reduces the problem to shorter prefixes, giving an optimal substructure recurrence.
Invariant: Every DP cell contains the minimum cost for its two prefixes, based on already computed shorter prefixes.
Edge cases: Empty prefixes cost the length of the other prefix. Equal strings return zero.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Space is O(mn) for the table.
complexity_reason: The table has (m+1)(n+1) prefix pairs, each filled in constant time.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
approach_name: Use first row and column as markers
notes:
Task and constraints: If any cell is zero, set its whole row and column to zero in place. The solution should use constant auxiliary space beyond the matrix.
Idea: Record whether the first row and first column originally contain zero. Use their remaining cells as markers for zeroes found in the interior, then zero marked rows and columns and finally handle the first row and column.
Technique and why it applies: The matrix itself can store the row/column flags, avoiding separate arrays of markers.
Invariant: Before the final clearing pass, matrix[r][0] and matrix[0][c] indicate whether row r or column c must become zero.
Edge cases: The original first row and first column need separate flags because they are also used as marker storage.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The first row and column store markers, with two booleans for their original state.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
notes:
Task and constraints: Search for a target in a matrix whose rows are sorted and whose first value in each row exceeds the previous row's last value.
Idea: Treat the m by n matrix as one sorted array of length mn. Binary-search a virtual index and map it to row index // n and column index % n.
Technique and why it applies: The row-boundary property guarantees the entire matrix is sorted in row-major order.
Invariant: If target exists, it remains within the current virtual-index interval.
Edge cases: A single-row or single-column matrix works with the same mapping. Values outside the global range return false.
Complexity: Time is O(log(mn)). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: A virtual flattened index maps directly to a matrix cell.

title: Sort Colors
notes:
Task and constraints: Sort an array containing only 0, 1, and 2 in place, in that order, without calling a general sorting function.
Idea: Maintain low, current, and high pointers. Move zeroes to the front, twos to the back, and advance current over ones.
Technique and why it applies: The three known categories can be partitioned in one pass using swaps and a boundary for each category.
Invariant: Values before low are zero, values between low and current are one, and values after high are two; the middle region is unclassified.
Edge cases: When current sees a two, swap with high and do not advance current because the swapped-in value is unclassified.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each pointer moves monotonically and each element is classified in place.

title: Minimum Window Substring
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the shortest substring of s containing every character in t with the required multiplicities. Return an empty string if no window satisfies the requirement.
Idea: Count required characters, expand the right boundary while recording counts, and shrink the left boundary while the window still satisfies all required counts. Save the shortest valid window.
Technique and why it applies: Window validity changes monotonically as characters are added or removed, so two pointers avoid examining every substring.
Invariant: formed tracks how many distinct required characters currently meet their required frequency; the window is valid when formed equals the number of required distinct characters.
Edge cases: Duplicate characters in t must be counted. If t is empty or longer than s, return an empty string.
Complexity: Time is O(|s|+|t|) expected. Extra space is O(character alphabet) for frequency maps.
complexity_reason: Both window pointers advance at most the length of s.

title: Combinations
notes:
Task and constraints: Return every combination of k distinct numbers chosen from 1 through n, with no regard to order within a combination.
Idea: Build a path in increasing order. At each depth choose a number greater than the previous choice, then recurse until the path length is k.
Technique and why it applies: Increasing choices prevent generating permutations of the same combination, while backtracking explores all valid selections.
Invariant: The path is strictly increasing and contains only values in [1,n].
Edge cases: k=n yields one combination containing every number. Prune when too few numbers remain to fill the path.
Complexity: Time is O(C(n,k)·k) to materialize all combinations. Auxiliary recursion space is O(k), excluding output.
complexity_reason: Each returned combination copies k values and recursion depth is k.

title: Subsets
notes:
Task and constraints: Return every subset of an array of distinct integers, including the empty set and the full array.
Idea: For each index, either include the current value in the path or skip it; record the path after all indices have been decided.
Technique and why it applies: Every element has two independent choices, so the recursion enumerates all 2^n subsets without duplication.
Invariant: The path contains only selected values from already processed indices, in original order.
Edge cases: The empty subset is a valid result. A one-element array returns the empty subset and the singleton subset.
Complexity: Time is O(n·2^n) to copy every subset. Auxiliary recursion space is O(n), excluding output.
complexity_reason: There are 2^n subsets and each output copy contains up to n values.

title: Word Search
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a word can be formed from horizontally or vertically adjacent board cells without reusing a cell in the same path.
Idea: Start DFS from each cell matching the first character. Match the next character in a neighboring cell, mark the current cell as used during recursion, and restore it on return.
Technique and why it applies: The board offers branching paths, and backtracking tests each legal neighbor while preventing reuse of the same cell.
Invariant: At recursion depth i, the path matches word[:i] and no board cell is used twice on that path.
Edge cases: If the word is longer than the number of cells, it cannot exist. Always restore a cell before returning from a failed branch.
Complexity: Worst-case time is O(mn·3^L) after the first step, where L is word length. Auxiliary recursion space is O(L).
complexity_reason: Each start cell explores adjacent paths of depth at most L.

title: Word Search
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a word can be formed from horizontally or vertically adjacent board cells without reusing a cell in the same path.
Idea: Start DFS from each cell matching the first character. Match the next character in a neighboring cell, mark the current cell as used during recursion, and restore it on return.
Technique and why it applies: The board offers branching paths, and backtracking tests each legal neighbor while preventing reuse of the same cell.
Invariant: At recursion depth i, the path matches word[:i] and no board cell is used twice on that path.
Edge cases: If the word is longer than the number of cells, it cannot exist. Always restore a cell before returning from a failed branch.
Complexity: Worst-case time is O(mn·3^L) after the first step, where L is word length. Auxiliary recursion space is O(L).
complexity_reason: Each start cell explores adjacent paths of depth at most L.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
approach_name: Allow a value twice in the prefix
notes:
Task and constraints: Modify a sorted array in place so each distinct value appears at most twice, preserving order, and return the valid prefix length.
Idea: Maintain a write index. A new value can be written if fewer than two values have been written or if it differs from the value two positions before the write index.
Technique and why it applies: Since the input is sorted, checking the element two slots back is enough to determine whether writing another copy would exceed two occurrences.
Invariant: The prefix before write is sorted and contains no value more than twice.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three already satisfy the rule. Values beyond the returned prefix are irrelevant.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: A single pass writes allowed values into the original array.
